meta.titre: Central Place Theory: settlement hierarchies, hexagons and K-values

sections.contenu_markdown: On market day, farmers from the villages of a Cameroonian division bring their produce to the nearest small town, but someone who needs a specialist doctor or a university may travel on to a regional capital such as Bamenda, Bafoussam or Douala. Settlements differ in size because they offer different services to the people around them. Examiners test this idea by asking you to identify the K-value of a hexagonal network, to state the assumptions of the model and to explain why real settlements are spaced irregularly. This course gives you the vocabulary, the three K-values and the arguments you need.

items: A settlement is a place where people live and work, from a hamlet or village to a town or a city.
The market area of a settlement is the area from which it draws its customers.
Population density is the number of people per square kilometre.
A regular hexagon is a six-sided shape that fits together with others without gaps.

sections.titre: Central place theory: threshold, range, hexagons and K-values
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms
- **Central place theory**: an explanation, first set out by the German geographer Walter Christaller, of the size, number and spacing of settlements in terms of the goods and services they supply to the people around them.
- **Central place**: a settlement that supplies goods and services to its surrounding area, called its **market area** or complementary region.
- **Order of a good**: low-order goods (bread, salt, a small shop) are bought often and cheaply; high-order goods and services (a specialist hospital, a university, jewellery) are bought rarely and cost more.
- **Threshold**: the minimum number of customers needed for a good or service to be supplied profitably. **Range**: the maximum distance people will travel to obtain it. A service survives only if the area inside its range holds at least the threshold population.
- **Hierarchy**: many small places offering only low-order services, and a few large places offering low-order and high-order ones.

### Assumptions of the model
An isolated, flat plain with the same soil and resources everywhere; population and purchasing power evenly spread; transport equally easy in every direction, with cost rising with distance; rational consumers who visit the nearest centre offering the good; suppliers who earn normal profit only.

### Hexagonal market areas and K-values
Circles leave gaps or overlap, so the model uses hexagons, which fit together with no gaps. The **K-value** is the number of lower-order market areas served by one higher-order centre, counting the lower-order area at its own centre.

| K | Principle | Position of lower-order centres | Calculation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Marketing | At the corners, each shared by three higher-order areas | $1 + 6 \times \frac{1}{3} = 3$ |
| 4 | Transport | At the midpoints of the sides, each shared by two areas and lying on main routes | $1 + 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4$ |
| 7 | Administrative | Wholly inside one hexagon, not shared | $1 + 6 \times 1 = 7$ |

A higher K means each higher-order centre controls a larger number of lower-order areas.

variantes.nom: Reading a K-value from a hexagonal network
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes where the smaller settlements lie around a central place.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Look at where the lower-order places sit. Corners shared by three hexagons: K = 3. Midpoints of the sides, usually on a road: K = 4. Inside the hexagon and not shared: K = 7. Then confirm with $K = 1 + 6 \times$ (share of each neighbour). Name the principle (marketing, transport or administrative) if the question asks.

variantes.nom: Why the pattern is hardly found in reality
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked for reasons or arguments why the predicted regular spacing is not observed.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give separate arguments, each linking a real-world factor to its effect on spacing: (1) relief, rivers and forests break up the flat plain, so settlements follow valleys and passes; (2) population and resources are unevenly spread, with mining, port or tourist towns appearing where resources are found; (3) transport routes are uneven, so towns grow at junctions and along roads; (4) governments and planners place towns, boundaries and services for political reasons; (5) people do not always shop at the nearest centre, because of income, taste and multi-purpose trips; (6) modern transport and the internet widen the range of high-order services; (7) history shapes where old towns grew. Develop each argument in one or two sentences.

sections.enonce_markdown: A regional planner draws a network in which each town stands at the centre of its own hexagonal market area. Small market villages lie at the midpoints of the sides of each hexagon, and each village is shared equally between two neighbouring towns. (a) Determine the K-value. (b) Name the principle that the network follows and explain why it suits places on main roads.

etapes.action: Read the position of the lower-order places.
etapes.justification: The K-value depends on where the villages lie and how many towns share them.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Villages at the midpoints of the sides, each shared equally by two towns.

etapes.action: Find the share of each neighbouring village that belongs to one town.
etapes.justification: A village shared by two towns gives each town one half of it.
A hexagon has six sides, so six midpoints and six shared villages.
K counts the central village area plus the shares of the six neighbours.

etapes.action: Name the principle and justify it.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Because villages lie on the sides of the hexagons, the main roads from town to town pass through them, so the most places are served by the fewest roads.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a) K = 4. (b) The transport principle**: lower-order places sit on the midpoints of the hexagon sides, on the main routes that link the higher-order centres, so the road network is as short as possible while serving the largest number of settlements.

items.erreur_markdown: "K = 3 means the hexagon contains three settlements."
items.pourquoi_faux: K is the number of lower-order market areas controlled by one higher-order centre (including its own), not a count of settlements on a map.
items.correction_markdown: Write that K = 3 means one centre serves itself and one third of each of six neighbours: $1 + 6 \times \frac{1}{3} = 3$.

items.erreur_markdown: Matching corners with the administrative principle and the interior with the marketing principle.
items.pourquoi_faux: The two are reversed: corners shared by three areas give K = 3 (marketing); lower-order places wholly inside the hexagon give K = 7 (administrative).
items.correction_markdown: Learn the pairs: corners = 3 = marketing; midpoints = 4 = transport; inside = 7 = administrative.

items.erreur_markdown: Defining threshold as the greatest distance people will travel.
items.pourquoi_faux: That is the range. The threshold is the minimum number of customers needed to make the service profitable.
items.correction_markdown: Write: threshold = minimum market (people); range = maximum distance.

items.erreur_markdown: Answering a question on why regular spacing is hardly found with "because it is only a theory".
items.pourquoi_faux: This gives no geographical argument and earns no marks. Each argument must name a factor and show how it distorts spacing.
items.correction_markdown: Write, for example: uneven population distribution means more settlements where people are concentrated, so spacing is irregular.

items.enonce_markdown: Define the terms threshold and range, and explain why a service is not supplied in a settlement if the range of the good is too short to reach the threshold population.
items.solution_markdown: **Threshold** is the minimum number of customers (population) needed to make a good or service profitable. **Range** is the maximum distance customers will travel to obtain it. Award marks for each definition. If the area within the range contains fewer people than the threshold, the supplier cannot make a profit, so **the service will not be supplied there** and customers must travel to a larger centre.

items.enonce_markdown: A pharmacy needs a threshold population of 6,000 people. Hexagonal market area X covers 150 km² with 55 people per km². Area Y also covers 150 km² but has 30 people per km². (a) Which area can support the pharmacy? (b) What is the lowest population density at which a 150 km² market area can support it?
items.solution_markdown: (a) Population of X = $150 \times 55 = 8\,250$, which is above 6,000, so X can support the pharmacy. Population of Y = $150 \times 30 = 4\,500$, which is below 6,000, so Y cannot. (b) Minimum density = $\frac{6\,000}{150} = 40$ people per km². **X can; the minimum density is 40 people per km².**

items.enonce_markdown: In a K = 4 network, (a) how many town market areas does one city market area contain, and how many village market areas, if each town area contains the same number of village areas as the city contains town areas? (b) Explain how better roads and widespread car ownership might change the pattern of central places.
items.solution_markdown: (a) A K = 4 city area contains **4 town areas**, and each town area contains 4 village areas, so the city contains $4 \times 4 = \mathbf{16}$ **village areas**. (b) Award marks for developed points: faster, cheaper travel increases the range of high-order goods; people bypass small centres to use larger ones; small shops and services lose customers and may close; larger centres grow and their market areas expand; the number of central places falls and the hierarchy becomes more concentrated.

items_markdown: Christaller's theory explains the size, number and spacing of settlements by the services they provide to the area around them.
Threshold is the minimum market needed; range is the maximum distance people will travel. A service needs the range to include the threshold population.
The model assumes a flat, uniform plain, evenly spread population and resources, equal transport costs in all directions and rational consumers.
K = 1 + 6 x (share of each neighbour): corners shared by three give K = 3 (marketing), midpoints shared by two give K = 4 (transport), places wholly inside give K = 7 (administrative).
Regular hexagonal patterns are hardly found because of relief, uneven population and resources, uneven transport, government decisions, consumer behaviour, technology and history.
